subject: Change point models w/ covariates determined by change point

messages.author: 96d103690e87b10f
messages.subject: Change point models w/ covariates determined by change point
parts:
Hey everyone, apologies if the answer to this is obvious but I'm struggling to determine the consequences of using a change point in a model that determines not only when parameter estimates should differ, but also how the data itself is summarized into covariates.

For example, let's say I have 2 predictors in a logistic regression model, predictor A and predictor Z.  I have values for these predictors in such a way that across a dataset consisting of 5,000 observations for 50 patients (it's a medical dataset with about 100 measurements per patient) predictor A is always the same for a given patient (as is the outcome) while predictor Z can fluctuate.  I suspect there is a point at which the effect of Z on the outcome dramatically changes, so I'm trying to determine where that split is and what the effects are above and below it.  For example the data may look like:

Patient ID   A       Z      Outcome
1                 1.1    10     1
1                 1.1    5       1
1                 1.1    8       1
...
50                -.8     3      0
50                -.8     21    0
50                -.8     17    0
# 5,000 records total

Now, in a more standard change point model I could say there is a single change point somewhere for Z and that the coefficient for Z above and below that value differs (I've seen plenty of examples out there like that), but that's not what I'm curious about.

What I'm really after though is an answer to this question:

Is it possible to have the change point in Z determine an aggregation over the values of Z for a given patient and then use those aggregations as covariates, instead of individual values?

For example, if the change point (which I'll call CP), for Z was say 5 I could then summarize the 5,000 record dataset into 50 observations and create two new variables like "Percentage of observations where Z was below CP=5" and "Percentage of observations where Z was above CP=5".  The new data used to generate the log probability in each step might then look like this:

Patient ID   A       pct_of_z_obs_below_CP   pct_of_z_obs_above_CP    Outcome
1                 1.1    .23                                      .77                                        1
2                 0.5    .56                                      .44                                        0
3                 1.9    .81                                      .19                                        0
...
50               -.8     .1                                        .9                                          1
# 50 records total

These values would then be passed into the likelihood function, after multiplying them by their coefficients.


Sure there are other ways to do the modeling that don't involve aggregations of covariates at each step, but for the sake of the mental exercise, is this approach ever valid?  I see that there are already some difficulties in sampling change points with Stan since they induce a discontinuity in the likelihood, but I have no clue what the consequences are of also manipulating the covariate values at each step.  Does anybody have experience with this?

I attached a model that would attempt to do this, if seeing it in code instead is of any help. 

Thanks!

Looks like nobody responded here. I've been trying to lay
off these complicated-looking modeling issue posts hoping
better statisticians would respond.

You can build the simple change-point model where each patient
has a change at some point or where there is a shared change.

I didn't understand your aggregation scheme, but if you can
write the likelihood down, you can probably code it in Stan.

And if it's really just a mental exercise, we're awfully busy
for that kind of thing! I think that's one reason I put this one
on the backburner.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks Bob!  Yea sorry "mental exercise" was probably a poor way to phrase it -- it is a real research problem and this is the best solution I've come across so I don't mean to propose it as a passing thought.

Maybe a better question, or at least one more specific to the mechanics of Stan, is:

If the likelihood is not continuously differentiable with respect to a certain parameter, is it absolutely necessary to manually marginalize over it (in the transformed parameters block)?

Or put another way, what are the consequences of just letting Stan randomly sample something like a change point?  In some small simulated datasets I created both approaches seem to work but I'm just not sure what to expect from Stan in that case with larger, more realistic datasets.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change point models w/ covariates determined by change point
parts:
> On Nov 20, 2015, at 7:55 AM, Eric Czech <eric.all...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob! Yea sorry "mental exercise" was probably a poor way to phrase it -- it is a real research problem and this is the best solution I've come across so I don't mean to propose it as a passing thought.
>
> Maybe a better question, or at least one more specific to the mechanics of Stan, is:
>
> If the likelihood is not continuously differentiable with respect to a certain parameter, is it absolutely necessary to manually marginalize over it (in the transformed parameters block)?

It depends. If it's just a small kink in an otherwise differentiable
function, that's one thing, but if it's a discontinuity in the underlying
function, then small step size won't cope.

> Or put another way, what are the consequences of just letting Stan randomly sample something like a change point? In some small simulated datasets I created both approaches seem to work but I'm just not sure what to expect from Stan in that case with larger, more realistic datasets.

Stan can't do discrete sampling. You can use a continuous
changepoint, then do conditionals, but there's no way to get
information back to the changepoint sampling that way, so it'll
reduce to an accept/rejection algorithm, which is bad news.

- Bob

messages.author: 96d103690e87b10f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change point models w/ covariates determined by change point
parts: Thanks again Bob.  For the sake of posterity, I've had much better success using nonlinear functions to model the change points instead, which also generalizes fairly well to having multiple change points as linear combinations of sigmoid curves.  Stan purrs right along now that everything is strictly differentiable and converges much faster given that I don't have ugly, manual marginalizations programmed in there.
